title: How to Open a Salon: A Step-by-Step Guide
summary: Thinking about opening a salon? This step-by-step guide covers startup costs, licensing, hiring, and everything else you need to open a salon the right way.
body_markdown:
The[US hair salon industry is worth $60 billion](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/industry/hair-salons/4410/) , counts more than one million businesses, and keeps growing. The[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm) projects 5 percent employment growth for hairstylists and cosmetologists between 2024 and 2034.


A growing industry doesn't guarantee a profitable business, though. Opening a salon takes more capital than most people budget, more licenses than they expect, and more operational complexity than many first-time owners anticipate. The owners who get it right aren't necessarily the most talented stylists. They're the ones who came in with a plan.


This guide covers everything you need to know about how to open up a salon from the ground up, from choosing your concept to opening your doors, including a full checklist at the end.


{{banner-cta}}


## **TL;DR: What It Takes to Open a Salon**


If you're mapping out how to open a salon business, whether from scratch or as a pivot from another industry, these are the nine steps that matter most before opening day:


1. Define your salon concept and business model
2. Write a salon business plan
3. Understand your startup costs and secure financing
4. Choose the right location
5. Get licensed, permitted, and insured
6. Design your space and order equipment
7. Hire and build your team
8. Set up your day-to-day operations
9. Market your salon and plan your grand opening


A home-based or salon suite setup can start as low as $10,000. A standard standalone salon typically runs $60,000 to $90,000, and can exceed $130,000 for larger or higher-end builds. Most first-time owners spend more than their initial estimate, so build in a buffer.


## **How to Open a Salon, Step by Step**


### **Step 1: Define your salon concept and business model.**


The steps for how to open a beauty salon, a hair salon, or a nail studio are broadly the same. The differences show up in licensing, equipment, and the clients you are building for.


Before you sign a lease or order a single chair, get clear on two things: what kind of salon you're opening, and how you'll structure your team.


**Type of salon.** Hair, nail, full-service beauty, wellness, and barber businesses all fall under the salon umbrella, and each comes with different licensing requirements, equipment costs, and client profiles. Your concept shapes your location, pricing, hiring, and equipment list. A budget-friendly cut-and-color shop and a luxury color destination aren't just different in feel. They're structurally different businesses.


**Staffing model.** This decision affects everything from your startup costs to your weekly operations.


Comparison of three salon staffing models: employees (W-2), booth renters (1099), and commission-based Staffing model How it works Best for


Employees (W-2) Most control over your team


- You set hours and assign shifts
- You provide equipment and tools
- You handle payroll taxes and withholding


- Building a consistent brand
- Training junior stylists


Booth renters (1099) Lowest overhead


- Stylists pay you a fixed weekly rental fee
- They keep their own clients and revenue
- They set their own hours


- Reducing upfront overhead risk
- Less day-to-day management


Commission-based Shared revenue model


Stylists earn a percentage of the services they perform — typically 40–60%. Sharing revenue as you build the clientele; a middle ground between full employment and booth rental.


Many first-time owners start with a[booth rental model](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/booth-rental-salon) to reduce overhead risk, then shift to employees as the business grows. The[difference between W-2 employees and 1099 contractors](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/1099-w2-employees-what-is-the-difference) goes beyond pay structure: it affects taxes, liability, and how much control you have over someone's hours. If you're exploring how to open a salon suite business rather than a standalone location, the booth renter model fits best.


### **Step 2: Write a salon business plan.**


A[salon business plan](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/salon-business-plan) forces you to work through the numbers on paper before you spend real money. A complete plan covers:


- **Executive summary:** what you're building and why
- **Market and competitor analysis:** who's in your area and where the gap is
- **Services menu and pricing:** what you'll charge and how it compares to the competition
- **Staffing plan:** your model, headcount, and compensation structure
- **Financial projections:** startup costs, monthly operating expenses, and a break-even estimate


That last one deserves real attention. Work out how many client services per day cover your rent, payroll, supplies, and insurance. If the math is tight before you sign anything, something in the plan needs to change.


A business plan is also what lenders want to see before they extend credit. Have one ready before you apply for an SBA loan.


### **Step 3: Understand your startup costs and secure financing.**


Opening a salon can cost anywhere from $10,000 to well over $200,000. A home-based or salon suite setup can start around $10,000 to $35,000.[According to Lendio](https://www.lendio.com/blog/cost-to-open-salon) , a small-to-medium standalone salon typically runs $60,000 to $90,000, and larger builds or premium markets can push costs to $130,000 or more before opening day. First-time owners routinely underestimate costs, so budget beyond your initial estimate.


The ranges below apply whether you are calculating how much it costs to open a hair salon or a beauty salon, with exact figures varying by market, build-out scope, and service offering.


**One-time startup costs:**


- Leasehold improvements and build-out: $5,000 to $50,000 or more
- Salon equipment (chairs, shampoo bowls, dryers, stations): $10,000 to $40,000
- Initial product inventory: $2,000 to $7,000
- Licenses and permits: $200 to $12,000, depending on your state
- Insurance, signage, and professional fees: varies


[Ongoing monthly costs](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/salon-monthly-expenses) **:**


- Rent: $1,500 to $4,000 depending on market
- Utilities: $300 to $1,500
- Product restocking: $1,500 to $2,500
- Booking and scheduling apps: $150 to $400


Experienced owners consistently report finishing their build-out over budget. The surprises are often plumbing, electrical upgrades, and permitting delays. Keep at least three to six months of operating expenses in reserve before you open.


**Funding options:**


- **Personal savings:** no debt, full control
- [SBA 7(a) loans](https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans) **:** up to $5 million for qualified businesses with a solid plan
- [SBA microloans](https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans/microloans) **:** up to $50,000 for smaller needs; the average microloan is around $13,000, with more accessible qualification requirements than conventional loans
- **Equipment financing:** borrow against specific equipment rather than the business overall


### **Step 4: Choose the right location.**


Location affects your startup costs and client volume at the same time. A downtown storefront costs more in rent but brings walk-in traffic. A suburban plaza is cheaper, but you'll need to work harder to build a book.


Before you commit to any space, evaluate four things:


- **Foot traffic and visibility:** can people find you easily, or do they have to seek you out?
- **Parking:** this matters more than most new owners expect, especially for longer appointments
- **Proximity to competition:** a little nearby competition validates demand; saturation is a warning sign
- **Zoning:** not every commercial or mixed-use space permits salon operations. Check with the local zoning office before you sign, not after.


Try to negotiate a rent-free period during build-out, a cap on annual increases, and renewal options. A commercial real estate attorney is worth the cost on a first lease.


Opening a salon suite is a simpler starting point if you're not ready for a full location: you rent a ready-made chair in a shared space, build a client base, and save capital before taking on your own lease.


### **Step 5: Get licensed, permitted, and insured.**


Licensing and permits take longer than most people expect. Start this process early.


**Do you need a cosmetology license to own a salon?** You don't need a cosmetology license to own a salon in most states, but you do need one if you plan to perform services yourself. Every licensed professional working in your salon, whether stylists, nail techs, or estheticians, must hold the appropriate state-issued license. Requirements vary by state, so check directly with your state cosmetology board.


**What you'll typically need:**


- **Business entity registration:** an LLC is the most common structure for liability protection, and you'll need an EIN if you're hiring anyone
- **Cosmetology establishment license:** required in most states to legally operate a salon, separate from individual stylist licenses, and it usually triggers a pre-opening inspection
- **Health department permit:** most states require an inspection covering sanitation, ventilation, chemical storage, and fire safety
- **Local business license:** required in most municipalities


If you're researching[how to open a nail salon](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/how-to-start-a-nail-salon) , note that nail and esthetics businesses have separate licensing tracks from hair salons in most states. Confirm your specific requirements directly with your state board.


**Insurance:** Budget for general liability, professional liability,[workers' compensation](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/workers-compensation-101-for-small-business-owners) (required in most states once you have employees), and property coverage. Combined, this typically runs $200 to $250 per month.


### **Step 6: Design your space and order equipment.**


Your salon's layout affects how quickly your team moves through clients. Plan for clearly defined areas for styling stations, shampoo stations, drying, waiting, and reception.


**Equipment you'll need:**


- Styling chairs and stations
- Shampoo bowls and chairs
- Hair dryers and hooded dryers (essential for color services)
- Mirrors and task lighting at each station
- Reception desk and waiting area seating
- POS hardware and storage


Order equipment at least eight to 12 weeks before opening. Popular styling chairs and custom stations can have long lead times, and delays push your opening date. Many salon suppliers offer wholesale pricing to licensed salon owners.


Once your equipment is confirmed and your layout is set, use the checklist at the end of this guide to track everything before opening day.


### **Step 7: Hire and build your team.**


Whether you're figuring out[how to open a hair salon](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/opening-a-hair-salon) or a full-service beauty salon, finding good stylists is harder than most new owners expect. Licensed stylists have options: other salons, booth rental elsewhere, independent studios. Your compensation, culture, and growth story all factor into whether someone chooses to build their career with you.


When hiring, look for:


- **Active, current license:** verify this before the interview stage
- **Technical skill** appropriate to your services menu
- **Client service orientation:** skill matters less if they can't build a book
- **Reliability:** ask specifically about their history of showing up consistently


For booth renters, focus on their existing client base. A renter who brings 30 loyal clients is a different hire than one starting from zero.


[Training beauty and wellness employees](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/how-to-train-beauty-wellness-employees) takes real effort even with experienced hires.[Good communication in a salon](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/good-communication-in-a-salon) has to be built from the start: scheduling systems, product protocols, and client expectations all take time to absorb, regardless of how long they've been behind a chair.


### **Step 8: Set up your day-to-day operations.**


Three systems every salon needs before the first client walks in.


**1. Appointment booking**


Clients should be able to book any time of day. Data from Phorest, analyzed across more than 5,000 salons and spas, shows that[about 46 percent of appointments](https://www.salontoday.com/articles/data-confirms-demand-for-online-booking) are booked when salons are closed. A[salon scheduling app](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/best-salon-scheduling-app) that syncs with each stylist's schedule prevents double-booking and cuts no-shows through automated reminders.


**2. Point-of-sale (POS) system**


Your POS handles service payments, retail product sales, tip distribution, and financial reporting. Connect it to your accounting tool so you're not manually entering transactions at the end of each day.


**3. Scheduling, time tracking, and payroll**


This is where new salon owners most often run into trouble. If you have a mix of commission employees, part-time hourly workers, and booth renters, you need a system that handles all three pay structures without manual math every pay period. Before committing to any tools, it's worth understanding[what each option actually handles](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/salon-management-software-solutions) , because scheduling alone won't cover payroll for booth renters, commission employees, and part-time hourly workers at the same time.


Luanne Ronquillo, owner and founder of Ruru Baked, laid out exactly what she needed when she evaluated her options: "The interface needs to be easy to use. It needs to have reporting so I can see our labor costs per day. And it needs to have things like availability that we can plug in. I want to be able to log in from multiple locations and have multiple locations within the same database. And then it needs to connect to QuickBooks so I can do payroll. Homebase had everything that I needed and was a good price."


Homebase connects scheduling, time clocks, and payroll in one app, so you can see your labor costs, approve hours, and run payroll without chasing down information at the end of every week.[Try Homebase for free.](https://app.joinhomebase.com/onboarding/sign-up)


### **Step 9: Market your salon and plan your grand opening.**


Marketing starts before you open. Make sure you get these prepped well:


- **Google Business Profile.** Set this up and fill it out completely: hours, services, location, photos. Research from SOCi shows that businesses in the Google Local 3-Pack receive[126 percent more traffic](https://searchengineland.com/guide/google-local-pack) than those just outside the top three results.
- **Social media.** Instagram and TikTok are the main channels for beauty businesses. Posting behind-the-scenes build-out content, coming-soon reels, and before-and-after work during your pre-launch phase builds an audience before your first appointment. Consistency matters more than production value early on.
- **Grand opening.** A[soft opening](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/what-is-a-soft-opening) two to four weeks before your official launch gives your team time to practice under real conditions. For the official date, a referral incentive, like "bring a friend and you both get 15 percent off," helps fill the book and activates word of mouth early.
- **Retention from day one.** An[analysis of more than 11 million appointments](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20231010624493/en) by Boulevard found that first-time clients who book online are roughly twice as likely to return for a second visit compared to walk-ins. Pre-booking at checkout is one of the highest-impact habits you can build into your process from the start.


## **Your Salon Opening Checklist**


Use this checklist to track your progress across every phase, from pre-planning to launch.


**Pre-planning**


- Defined your salon concept and type
- Chosen your staffing model
- Written a business plan with projections and a break-even estimate
- Estimated startup costs with a buffer built in
- Identified your funding sources


**Setup**


- Signed a lease or confirmed a salon suite arrangement
- Verified zoning allows salon operations at your location
- Registered your business entity and applied for an EIN
- Applied for a cosmetology establishment license
- Scheduled your health department inspection
- Secured all required insurance coverage
- Completed space design and layout
- Ordered all salon equipment (eight to 12 weeks out)


**Staffing and systems**


- Posted job listings and interviewed candidates
- Verified each hire's active cosmetology license
- Completed onboarding paperwork
- Set up appointment booking, POS, and team management tools


**Launch**


- Created and optimized your Google Business Profile
- Set up Instagram and TikTok and started posting
- Ran a soft opening
- Planned your grand opening event and referral offer


## **FAQs about Opening a Salon**


### How much does it cost to open a salon?


A home-based or salon suite setup can start around $10,000 to $35,000. A small-to-medium standalone salon typically runs $60,000 to $90,000, and larger or higher-end builds can exceed $130,000. Expect to go over your initial estimate. Experienced owners consistently report finishing their build-out over budget, which is why keeping three to six months of operating expenses in reserve matters.


### How do I make $100,000 as a hairstylist?


It typically requires a combination of high service volume, a disciplined retail sales habit, and either raising prices or moving to a higher-end environment. Booth rental can accelerate this by giving stylists full control over their pricing and schedule. Most stylists who reach this number have a loyal, established client base with few gaps in their books.


### Is owning a salon profitable?


It can be, but margins are tight.[Industry data](https://thesalonbusiness.com/salon-revenue-model/) commonly cites net margins around eight percent for hair salons. The most profitable salons combine strong client retention, retail product sales, and efficient labor management. Booth rental models often produce more predictable margins because rental income is fixed regardless of service volume.


### How do I open my own salon with no money?


If you're exploring how to open a salon with no money, start smaller than a full storefront. Renting a booth or suite in an existing salon lets you build a client base and save capital before committing to a lease.[SBA microloans](https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans/microloans) of up to $50,000 are built for early-stage needs, with more accessible qualification requirements than conventional loans. Some owners launch from a home-based salon in jurisdictions that allow it and scale up from there.


### How long does it take to open a salon?


Most salons take three to six months from lease signing to opening day, assuming no major permitting delays. The timeline depends on build-out scope, equipment lead times, and how long your state's licensing and inspection process takes.


### What is the most profitable type of salon to open?


Hair salons tend to generate the highest revenue because clients return regularly for cuts and color. Nail salons often have lower overhead and strong repeat business. Booth rental models, regardless of salon type, tend to produce the most consistent margins because rental income doesn't depend on service volume.
